confirmed.claim: (a) is open because entity fields prove that owned linkable locations can be created lazily.
confirmed.finding: An entity field is `createWritableProjection(computeField, writeField)` stamped with the collection's registry (definePositionRegistry) and an entity binding. It has no storage or position of its own. Link delivers it by filtering the collection's notifications on owner position, subjectId and fieldKey footprint, and by reading the row payload. This proves that a lazily created accessor over existing owned storage can be linked. It does not prove that new owned state, such as an exposable frontier, can be created lazily.

The correction: the probe does create new owned state after construction. `addOne` at option-a-lazy-location.mjs:28 adds a new subject (a row). But that row sits inside a collection declared at construction, and its changes go out on that collection's existing notification channel. So the auditor's "does not prove new owned state can be created lazily" is too absolute. The accurate statement is narrower: the probe does not show that a new kind of owned location can be created lazily and delivered, meaning one outside the leaf and collection channels, which is what an exposable frontier would be. The addition, which is the stronger gap: link() reads the accessor only once, when the link is created (link.ts:308). After that it takes the value it sends from the collection's notification payload, `v[fieldKey]` (link.ts:495-500). So the entity-field case shows Link delivering the value that was written, never a projection's computed value. An exposable frontier is exactly a projection whose value differs from what was written (the commit 9df8fbff message says so itself). The precedent therefore does not carry over to delivery. Option (a) still needs a new emission channel that carries the exposable value and meets the L19 dormant seam, on top of the settlement-direction question. D3(a) should read: "open, but unproven. The probe shows only that link() accepts and delivers through a lazily created handle over existing collection storage and its emission channel."
check.reason: Every piece of the auditor's evidence checks out. The entity field is `createWritableProjection(computeField, writeField)`. It borrows the collection's registry through `definePositionRegistry` and gets an entity binding (entity-signal.ts:1815-1854), so it has no storage or position of its own. link() lets it through on metadata alone: a registry plus either an entity binding or a node address (link.ts:239-263). Delivery runs through a dedicated `entityLocation` branch. That branch filters the collection's notifications on owner position, subjectId and the fieldKey footprint (link.ts:474-504). The inference from "a lazily created accessor can be linked" to "a lazy exposable frontier is feasible" is therefore overstated. The one overreach in the finding is its absolute "no new owned state" wording, since `addOne` does create a new subject after construction. It is a small point, and it does not rescue option (a). The finding also missed that the delivered value is the notification payload (the written value), which is the opposite of what an exposable frontier needs. confirmed.claim: (a) is blocked because Link writes back and a projection can't take writes.
confirmed.finding: The mechanism is misplaced. The precedent itself is a writable projection: writeField delegates to api.updateOne. Link writes back only through acquire(), which only subscribe() and retrieve() call. A set-only endpoint is already accepted and never writes back. The real obstacle, shared by (a) and (b), is that Link's outbound path runs on path-notifier emissions from armed owned leaves, never on reactive reads of the source. An exposable value that changes when an obligation resolves emits no notification. So (a) also needs a kernel writer or emitter driven by obligation resolution. That is the same resolution-to-consumer index (a waiter) as (c), so (a) does not delete the waiter either.

The precedent is also a writable projection: its read is computeField and its writes go through writeField to api.updateOne (entity-signal.ts:1829-1856; the updateOne call is at :1848, just past the auditor's cited range). What 9df8fbff calls "settlement direction" therefore comes down to an admission rule: refuse get/subscribe on a frontier location, or send inbound writes to the ordinary location.

The real obstacle is how outbound works. Link's eligible value advances only from path-notifier emissions (:463-568, flushed via onFlush at :701) and from the collection order-capture channel (:703-738). It never re-reads the source; read() runs once, at creation (:308). Kernel confirm emits no path notification: confirmPending, then pendingConfirmedListeners, then settleCommitScope (transactions.ts:2700-2733). So a frontier value that changes when an obligation resolves reaches no Link unless a kernel writer or emitter driven by resolution exists. That is a waiter, so (a) does not delete the waiter.

The auditor also missed one point. Even with such an emitter, (a)'s send still goes through scheduleDurableConsequence with the source as claimant (link.ts:593-595, :651-653). A lazily bound location shares the tree's registry (entity-signal.ts:1819). While any scope is open, the send is held tree-wide (commit-consequence.ts:211-219). So (a) also needs the D4/F5 gate change, which makes it (c)'s gate plus a resolution-driven emitter, strictly more machinery than (c).

One overstatement to soften: "the same index as (c)". (a) would map resolution to affected frontier locations. (c) parks consequence closures and runs them on release (WAKEUP-3). Both are resolution-driven wakeups, but they are not the same structure.

check.corrected_finding:
The finding holds, and it understates the problem. No signature changes, but calling the v15 patch "no API change" is overstated, because two published behaviours change.

(1) The `retention.truncated` flag returned by `confirmedTurnReader` (from `@signal-tree/kernel/internals`, which that file's header calls a supported, stable seam for tooling) flips from true to false after an ordinary write on a tree with no history contract. The reader then returns `{turns: [], truncated: false}`. That is exactly the "live, enhancer present, nothing committed" answer an idle tree gives, and the reader docs warn against that kind of confident wrong answer.

The patch cannot simply "set it deliberately" either. The whole point of the patch is to make the `'**'` subscription lazy, so transactions would never see the ordinary write. Setting `evictedConfirmed` at install time instead would break the other pinned spec, "an untouched tree is NOT truncated". So at least one of two existing v15 specs must be changed: history-retention-15.spec.ts:127-132 or :134-137.

(2) Ordinary writes stop consuming turn ids (`nextTurnId++` in `buildTurn`), so later transaction turns get renumbered in default mode. This is visible in the reader's `turns[].id` and `firstAvailableTurnId`. It is also visible on the ROOT public API: `SignalTreeRollbackError` (exported from index.ts:92) carries `cause.pendingTurnId` and `conflictingTurnId`, and `explainRollbackFailure` puts "turn N" into the error message.

Mitigation: turn ids are already documented as gappy (confirmed-turn-view.ts:54-55), so renumbering is low severity. The truncated flip is the substantive contract change. The grid should say "no signature change; changes the reader's truncated semantics and turn numbering; requires amending a pinned v15 spec".
check.reason:
I confirmed every cited fact myself.

- **Export:** v15.3.0 package.json exports `./internals`, and `confirmedTurnReader` lives there.

That sets `evictedConfirmed`, and `getConfirmedRetention` reports it as `truncated`.
- **The pinned spec:** it exists at v15.3.0 and on main with identical lines, and it passes on main.

What the auditor missed:
- **Lazy subscription:** the patch as framed in 70b465b5 makes the `'**'` subscription lazy. Without observing the write, the patch cannot "deliberately" keep `truncated` true, and forcing it true at install breaks the adjacent "untouched tree" spec. So a pinned spec must change either way.
- **Root API:** turn ids also reach the root public API through `SignalTreeRollbackError`'s message and cause, not only the internals reader.

The finding is not refuted. It is correct in substance, and the corrections above extend it.

refuted.claim: (implicit) the lazy design is just deferring the '**' subscription like the enqueue observer
refuted.finding: If subscribe and onFlush become lazy but the interceptor branch keeps capturing idle writes into pendingCapture, those stale effects pile up. They get drained into the first record made after a turn opens (the '**' handler sets selfDirty). That record's id is higher than the pending turn's, so getPendingRollbackPlan treats it as a later authored turn and could refuse a rollback for a dependency that does not exist. I worked this out from the code; I have not reproduced it end to end.
refuted.evidence: transactions.ts:2316-2327 (interceptor non-transaction branch writes pendingCapture unconditionally), 2250 (selfDirty set only by the '**' handler), 2342-2347 (drain only on flush), 904-907 (authoredLater = confirmedTurns.filter(t => t.id > turnId))
refuted.grid_change: Add an implementation requirement: while idle, pendingCapture must not be written, or must be cleared when a transaction opens, before any record is made.

check.reason: The auditor read the code correctly: the interceptor's non-transaction branch (transactions.ts:2315-2327) does write into pendingCapture without any condition, and only the '**' handler sets selfDirty (2250). The hazard still does not happen, because ordinary writes in a transactions tree never reach that branch with an effect. transactions() declares capability 'causal-runtime' (transactions.ts:3112). That capability requires 'mutation-capture' (tree-capabilities.ts:16), so every owned leaf is wrapped by wrapOwnedWritableSignal and marked as having an intrinsic emitter (signal-tree.ts:207-218, owned-mutation.ts:246). interceptLeafSignals skips any node with that mark (intercept-leaf-signals.ts:248-251 and 268-271), so those writes reach transactions only through the '**' subscription. If that subscription is lazy, they are captured nowhere and nothing goes stale. The only built-in nodes that do reach the branch are entityMap mutator wrappers (wrapMutator, 211-230). Those pass undefined snapshots, because entityMap has __findKeyBySubjectId, and the ambient meta carries no structuralEffect after the method returns. So captureEffects returns early at `next === undefined && prev === undefined` (transactions.ts:1499-1501) and nothing is queued. Measured with an esbuild bundle of the unmodified kernel source, instrumented only with counters; no timing was run. pendingCapture stayed at 0 straight after every kind of ordinary write, and it is filled synchronously, so this is exactly what a lazy design would accumulate. A variant with the '**' subscription made lazy (registered in ensureEnqueueObserver, when a transaction opens) ran the auditor's scenario (idle write, open a turn, unrelated ordinary write, rollback) end to end, and the rollback settled correctly. There is a residual point, low severity and not a medium correctness gap: a lazy design should still gate this branch, or clear pendingCapture when it activates, as a defence for custom or unowned signals that carry position ids (not shown to be reachable). If such a stale effect did exist, it would come from a .set()/callable write with intent 'replace'. That stale effect would be classified as 'superseded' (transactions.ts:377-382, 560-562), and the rollback would silently leave the speculative value in place. So the auditor's prediction of a false refusal was also the wrong outcome.
check.evidence:
Code: transactions.ts:3112 `capabilities: ['causal-runtime']`; tree-capabilities.ts:16 `'causal-runtime': ['mutation-capture', 'position-topology']`; signal-tree.ts:207-218 `if (buildPlan.has('mutation-capture')) { wrapOwnedWritableSignal(leaf, ...) }`; owned-mutation.ts:246 `defineIntrinsicMutationEmitter(leaf ...)`; intercept-leaf-signals.ts:248-251 `if (isWritableLocation(node)) { if (!hasIntrinsicMutationEmitter(node)) observeLocation(...); return false; }` and 268-271 `if (hasOwnedMutationEmitter) return false;`; intercept-leaf-signals.ts:213-230 (wrapMutator passes undefined snapshots when __findKeyBySubjectId exists); transactions.ts:1499-1501 (captureEffects returns early when next and prev are both undefined); transactions.ts:377-382 (a later 'replace' set is classified superseded) and 560-562 (a superseded effect is skipped, not compensated).
Probe (scratchpad/lazy/probe.mjs and probe2.mjs; esbuild bundle of the repo source, with counters patched into the bundle only, no repo file touched, no timing). In the BASE variant, pendingCapture.effects.size read synchronously after each write was 0 for callable x(1), x(fn), nested a.b(1), deep leaf, Date, array, Map, branch write, root write, and entity addOne/updateOne/removeOne/setAll/clear. critic.claim: The six older open decisions (callback recovery, open-key Record, inspection paths, bundle budget, production diagnostics, hosted-benchmark auth) aren't affected by this work.
critic.finding: Callback recovery is affected. The throwing-subscriber strand the auditors found is the same failure class as that open row: transact() throws and no handle is returned. The subscriber's error escapes the post-callback flushSync before materializePendingTransaction runs and before the handle is built. PathNotifier does not isolate subscriber errors. Neither option in the row covers this. The conservative option ('expose the same retained handle on the existing error') is written for callback throws, not for a notifier-subscriber throw after a callback that succeeded. The alternative (catch inside the callback) cannot help, because the user's fn never threw. restoration's 'staged' handler also calls flushSync, which is a second throw point.
critic.evidence: open-decisions.md:9 (row text); transactions.ts:2663 flushSync, :2664 materializePendingTransaction, :2680 `const handle = {`; path-notifier.ts:401-419 subscriber loop with no try/catch; restoration.ts:3740 `getPathNotifier()?.flushSync()` in the lifecycle 'staged' handler
critic.grid_change: Remove callback recovery from the 'unaffected' list. Record that the recovery-contract decision must also cover a throw from a notifier subscriber during transact()'s post-callback flush, or that this path gets error isolation first.

critic.claim: Production diagnostics is not affected by this work.
critic.finding: D1's payoff depends on it. devTools() switches to its no-op only when `ngDevMode` is defined as false. When ngDevMode is undefined, which is the default outside Angular (React, Vue, Solid) unless the bundler defines it, the full implementation installs. It is enabled by default and subscribes '**' and onFlush permanently. That makes the process-global hasPathObservers() true, so every mutation-capture tree keeps emitting. Its interceptLeafSignals wrapper also calls notify on every write. So in any non-Angular production build that keeps devTools() and does not define ngDevMode=false, D1 saves nothing. Whether automatic removal is guaranteed is exactly what the Production diagnostics row leaves open.
critic.evidence: devtools.ts:63-66 (`typeof ngDevMode !== 'undefined' && !ngDevMode ? prodNoopDevTools : createDevToolsEnhancer`); devtools-impl.ts:1197 (`enabled = true` default), :1232, :1843-1848 (interceptLeafSignals -> notifier.notify), :1860 subscribe('**'), :1874 onFlush; open-decisions.md:12 ('NODE_ENV-only automatic removal is not universally established')
critic.grid_change: Couple D1 to Production diagnostics: the D1 gain is conditional on devTools() being folded out (explicit ngDevMode=false) in every framework's production build. The D2 gate needs an arm with devTools() present in a production-mode build.

critic.claim: Open-key Record topology and Bundle cost are not affected by this work.
critic.finding: (1) Open-key Record is coupled to D3(a). Its conservative option, 'dynamic descendant materialization', is a runtime mechanism for creating owned locations after construction. REGISTER's elimination of contribution-store rested on the absence of such a mechanism ('no API adds an owned location after construction'). 9df8fbff showed lazy creation only for entity fields, not plain paths. Choosing that option would supply the missing substrate for D3(a) on plain paths, and choosing against it limits D3(a) to entity fields. (2) Bundle cost is coupled to D1, D3 and D4. The prod budgets are already red. D1's per-owner guard would live in owned-mutation / path-observation-port, which the bare signal-tree.ts imports directly. The D3/D4 gate lives in commit-consequence, which link imports. Every byte those designs add lands on a red ceiling. No auditor sized this.

critic.claim: D1 is an open L15 owner decision: must an ordinary write made while no transaction is pending create a confirmed-turn record?
critic.finding: The L15 retention boundary is already marked SETTLED in the owner-decisions table: correctness-only by default, and records kept only while live obligations need them. Under that settled rule, an idle ordinary write is already released in the same recordConfirmed call. Presenting D1 as the L15 question invites re-deciding a settled boundary. What is actually open is narrower and follows from it: whether idle writes must still set the `truncated` latch and consume turn ids. That is an observation contract, not a retention one.

critic.claim: Adopt L19 ('an unused capability must cost nothing') as a law.
critic.finding: The frozen constitution forbids this as written. LAWS.md freezes L1-L18 and says no further laws are added speculatively. L19 also overlaps frozen L15: L15 already governs 'state retained for correctness ... only while a live semantic obligation requires it', and L19 extends that from retention to allocation and hot-path CPU. critic.claim: L19 as a law plus D1 as the repair makes an idle transactions() tree conform.
critic.finding: L19's own text sets 'enabled but unused' at 'at most a predictable branch'. No D1 variant reaches that, because the per-write mutation-capture wrapper is installed on every leaf at build time for any tree whose enhancers request causal-runtime, and only transactions() and restoration() request it. Each wrapped write still runs the observer path. With every registration and emission removed, the ablation still measures a residual of about +38% (an upper bound). If L19 were adopted today, released v15.3.0 would violate it, and so would HEAD after D1 and a per-owner guard. The only fix is to install the wrapper lazily, at promotion, which is a build-plan change appearing in no decision.

critic.claim: Add a CI benchmark gate using paired trials; the d2218eb0 regression went unnoticed because nothing measured idle cost.
critic.finding: (1) The repo has an explicit policy against timing assertions in gates. Measurement gates check the harness, not its numbers, and one is marked 'NOT a performance budget and must not become one'. The precedent for performance work (C6) split the gate: a deterministic invariant spec is the real gate, and timing is characterization only. A paired-trial timing gate reverses that policy without saying so. (2) A CI timing gate already exists: perf-suite.yml runs on push to main with PERF_FAIL_ON_VIOLATION=1 and a 25% overhead budget. It ran green through the whole regressed window, with d2218eb0 already on origin/main, because none of its arms installs an enhancer. So the accurate cause is 'the only CI timing gate has no enhancer arm', plus an explicitly unreviewed snapshot being merged (next finding). A deterministic invariant would have caught d2218eb0 directly, for example 'an idle transactions() tree registers no notifier observer', like 45f4ed8e's 'idle tree never registers' spec.

critic.finding: d2218eb0 is an explicitly unreviewed 'protective snapshot' ('NOT a reviewed change set ... must not be treated as approved'). It touched 125 kernel files and was merged into main by 0ce2a320. Besides observeEnqueue, it changed entity-signal.ts (+153 lines), path-notifier.ts (+154), link.ts (+427), commit-consequence.ts, signal-tree.ts and tree-realization-adapter.ts. The bisect and targeted ablation measured only scalar-leaf dormant writes. Only the serialization deletion got a later review. So the claim holds for the scalar dormant path. critic.claim: The L19 measurements characterize dormant cost (implicitly: for the workloads that matter).
critic.finding: No probe measures entity writes or more than one tree, and both change the result. The delivery runtime is installed process-wide the first time anything calls getPathNotifier() (transactions, restoration, devtools or link). After that, PORT.notify forwards every entity write from every tree, including unenhanced ones, and PathNotifier.notify has no observer short-circuit. So installing transactions() on one tree makes entity writes in unrelated trees enqueue and schedule a flush. Every transactions tree's '**' handler also receives all trees' writes and filters inside the handler, so flush cost grows with the number of transactions trees (SSR requests, component stores). The repo has already measured this cost class once, for restoration's onFlush, as 'cost that scales with OTHER people's trees'.
critic.evidence: path-observation-port.ts:78-86 (installPathDeliveryRuntime), :124-135 (PORT.notify forwards unconditionally); path-notifier.ts:239-300 (no hasObservers check), :837 (install); transactions.ts:2167-2185 (owner filtering inside the '**' handler); restoration.ts:4099-4105 (0.008 -> 9.7ms with 1-3 unrelated trees); l19-ablation-0b.mjs:38 and l19-dormant-cost use a single scalar tree
critic.grid_change: D2's gate and D1's claimed benefit need three arms: entity writes on a dormant tree; an unenhanced tree beside a dormant transactions tree; and K dormant transactions trees in one process.

critic.claim: (Auditor) restoration() is active by design because it records every write, so its cost is not a dormant L19 violation.
critic.finding: restoration() records only explicitly designated turns, via undoable(). A tree with restoration() and no designation is a 'configured-unused' capability, and the repo's own idle spec asserts it retains no history. Yet it registers '**' and onFlush eagerly and requests causal-runtime, so it pays the same wrapper and emission cost as dormant transactions(). It also keeps hasPathObservers() true for every tree in the process. It is therefore a second L19 dormant case, and it needs its own version of D1 (must undesignated writes be observed while nothing is designated?). The auditor's related point stands: without that decision, D1's gain disappears in any app that also uses restoration().

critic.claim: Lazy registration of transactions' '**' subscription (and onFlush) is behaviour-neutral apart from the recording decision.
critic.finding: Re-registering changes delivery order. PathNotifier delivers subscribers in Set insertion order, with no per-handler try/catch. subscribeCollectionNotifications unsubscribes and re-adds, so re-arming at transact() would move transactions' '**' handler behind every link(), observeWrites or devtools subscriber registered since install. Today it usually runs first. That handler is what captures in-transaction and later-while-pending writes at flush. So a throwing earlier subscriber would now pre-empt transactions' capture of that entry. The underlying problem is the missing isolation, which the auditors already reported. D1 makes it slightly worse. The onReset hook also re-subscribes '**' eagerly, so a notifier reset would silently undo the lazy registration.
critic.evidence: path-notifier.ts:128 (`subscribers = new Map<string, Set<...>>`), :401-419 (no try/catch); transactions.ts:2150-2152 (unsubscribe, then subscribe('**')), :2232-2245 (captureIntoBucket for transactionId in the '**' handler), :2265-2268 (onReset -> subscribeCollectionNotifications)
critic.grid_change: D1 design requirements: add per-handler error isolation in PathNotifier delivery before or with lazy registration, and make the onReset path respect the lazy state.
